fields.title: Your Mission: Find Our Island Home
fields.content:
Your task: help a new explorer find the Philippines and explain how island communities can be connected. You will use a map, follow a worked example, and solve a location challenge.

Start with the regional map. The green islands show the Philippines, a country in Southeast Asia. An archipelago is a group of islands. An island is land surrounded by water. These are different ideas: one island is a piece of land; an archipelago includes many islands.

The Philippines lies north of the Equator, an imaginary line around the middle of Earth. Nearby land helps us describe its location. A map is a model, so this small map leaves out many small islands. Modern place names help us locate places; they do not show every community that lived long ago.

fields.title: Watch How: Use the North Arrow
fields.content:
A worked example shows the steps before you try them. Question: where is Manila compared with Cebu City? These modern city names are reference points, not claims about ancient cities.

Step 1. Read the north arrow. It points toward the top of this map. South is the opposite direction. East is to the right and west is to the left on this north-up map.

Step 2. Find the two labelled dots: Manila and Cebu City. Compare the dots, not the ends of their text labels.

Step 3. Manila is higher on this map than Cebu City. We can say Manila is north of Cebu City. It is also farther west, but our question asks about the north-south relationship.

Step 4. Check the arrow again. Turning the page does not change where north is. Now use the same steps with a different pair of places.

fields.title: Try Together: Locate the Island Groups
fields.content:
Luzon, Visayas and Mindanao are the three major island groups commonly used to describe the Philippines. Look at their labels on the map. The labels show general locations, not lines dividing every island or community.

Let us work through one example together. Start at the Visayas label. Follow north on the map. You reach the broad area labelled Luzon. Follow south from the Visayas and you reach Mindanao.

An island-group name does not tell us every language, job or custom of the people living there. Each group contains different places and communities. Do not use one picture of a house or one costume as a description of everyone.

Your next task is about location. Use the map to decide which group lies between the other two in a general north-to-south description.

fields.title: Make a Plan: Surroundings and Livelihood
fields.content:
A location can offer resources and routes. Coastal water can support fishing and boat travel. Suitable farmland can support crops. People also need skills, tools and choices: living near the sea does not mean every person is a fisher.

The Philippines has a tropical, maritime climate. Tropical means it lies in the warm part of Earth near the Equator. Maritime means the surrounding seas influence its climate. Many places are warm and humid, but rainfall and local conditions differ. Climate describes patterns over many years; weather describes conditions at a particular time. A map alone cannot tell us tomorrow's weather.

Worked example: a made-up island community has fish, skilled basket makers and visiting boats. Another community grows grain. They could exchange products. The plan connects resources, skills and travel, without assuming everyone does one job.

fields.title: Your Turn: Write a Map Report
fields.content:
Now try a location problem without a worked answer beside it. Your task: help an explorer describe a possible journey from Manila to Cebu City. Start with the legend and north arrow, then compare the two dots.

The legend explains the map's colours: green shows Philippine land and blue shows water. The dots mark modern reference locations. A label names a place; it is not the place's full size or boundary.

Use what the map really shows. You can compare north and south, notice water between islands, and connect places with their island groups. You cannot work out an exact travel time or prove an ancient boat took a particular route from this locator.

Open the evidence cards, then choose the report that matches the map. You may look back at the north-arrow example if you need help.

fields.title: Field Journal: Connect Your Discoveries
fields.content:
Return to your mission problem: how can we locate our island home and explain connections between communities?

Your field journal now has five ideas. The Philippines is an archipelago in Southeast Asia. A north arrow helps you compare directions. Luzon, Visayas and Mindanao locate broad island groups. Surroundings offer resources and routes, while people contribute skills and choices. A map legend explains symbols, and a map has limits.

Connect the ideas: water separates islands, but boats can connect people. Communities can use different skills and resources and exchange products. We should not assume that every island has one livelihood or the same customs.

Before the quiz, check your explanation against the map. If directions are confusing, revisit the worked example. If a word is unfamiliar, use the Explain button for authored help. The quiz asks about ideas taught in this mission; passing does not mean you know all Philippine history.
